title: Common Attacks
subtitle: Attack identification table, malware family tree, SQLi/XSS/MITM & defence mapping

readingSections.title: The Attack Landscape
readingSections.quickSummary: Every attack has a one-line definition; AXIS PYQs test exactly that line - match the stem phrase to the name.
content: Network attacks fall into families: identity attacks (spoofing, phishing), availability attacks (DoS, DDoS, smurfing, email bombing), interception (man-in-the-middle, eavesdropping), code attacks (malware, SQL injection, XSS), and credential attacks (brute force, keylogging).

AXIS PYQs are identification drills: a one-line symptom appears, and you must name the attack. The published pool is small - spoofing, email bombing, phishing, smurfing, DDoS, and the malware quartet cover nearly every instance.
The defence mapping matters too: firewalls and filters against traffic attacks, antivirus against malware, user training against phishing, encryption against interception.

subsections.title: The core table (memorise verbatim)
subsections.content:
Spoofing - attacker creates a packet/identity that APPEARS to be something else.
Email bombing - flooding a user with massive unwanted email volume.
Phishing - fraudulent messages tricking users into revealing credentials.
Smurfing - ICMP echo to a broadcast address with a SPOOFED source; all hosts reply to the victim.
DoS/DDoS - overwhelming a service; DDoS = distributed across many machines.
Man-in-the-Middle - secretly relaying/altering traffic between two parties.

quickRevision: 'Appears to be something else' = spoofing. 'Unwanted volume of emails' = email bombing.
DDoS = DoS from many sources at once.
Smurfing = ICMP broadcast amplification + spoofed source.
Phishing targets PEOPLE; spoofing targets IDENTITIES/PACKETS.
tricks: Email vs traffic: mail-flood stems -> email bombing; bandwidth-flood stems -> DoS/DDoS/ping storm.
Two-technique questions: smurfing ALWAYS involves spoofing (forged source) - 'which two attacks...' answers pair them.
Human-gullibility stems -> phishing; technical-forgery stems -> spoofing.
patterns: 'User receives unwanted amount of emails' -> email bombing (published PYQ).
'Creates a packet that appears to be something else' -> spoofing (published PYQ).
'Thousands of machines flood one server' -> DDoS.

readingSections.title: The Malware Family Tree
readingSections.quickSummary: Virus needs a host file; worm self-spreads; trojan disguises; ransomware extorts; spyware/keyloggers watch; rootkits hide.
content: Malware = malicious software, sorted by BEHAVIOUR. Virus: attaches to a host FILE and spreads when that file runs - needs human action. Worm: self-replicates across networks WITHOUT any host file - pure network spread. Trojan horse: disguises itself as legitimate software; the user installs it willingly.

Ransomware encrypts the victim's data and demands payment - the extortion model. Spyware silently collects information; keyloggers record keystrokes (credential theft); adware force-feeds advertisements; rootkits bury themselves deep in the OS to hide other malware; botlets-turned-botnets turn infected machines into DDoS soldiers.
Defences map one-to-one: antivirus/anti-malware scanners, patches against worm-exploited vulnerabilities, download discipline against trojans, offline backups against ransomware.

subsections.title: The quartet compared
subsections.content:
Virus - attaches to host files; spreads by execution/sharing.
Worm - self-propagates over the network; no host needed.
Trojan - disguised as useful software; user installs it.
Ransomware - encrypts data; demands payment.

quickRevision: Host file needed = virus; network self-spread = worm; disguise = trojan; extortion = ransomware.
Keylogger = keystroke thief. Spyware = information thief. Rootkit = hider.
tricks: 'Needs a host file' vs 'self-replicates without host' is THE virus/worm discriminator - options always include both.
'Demands payment to unlock' -> ransomware, no other option qualifies.
patterns: 'Which malware spreads without human action?' - worm.

pyqPatterns.question: Difference between virus and worm?
pyqPatterns.approach: Host-file dependency vs autonomous network replication.

readingSections.companyNote: The virus/worm/trojan trio appears in every technical MCQ round of every company - highest-frequency malware question.

readingSections.title: Web & Code Attacks: SQLi, XSS, MITM
readingSections.quickSummary: SQL injection smuggles database commands through input fields; XSS injects scripts into trusted pages; MITM relays traffic secretly.
content: SQL injection (SQLi) exploits unsanitised input: an attacker types SQL fragments into a login or search field, and the backend executes them - classic payload ' OR 1=1 -- logs anyone in. Defence: parameterised queries and input validation.

Cross-site scripting (XSS) injects malicious JavaScript into pages OTHER users trust - stolen cookies and session hijacking follow. Defence: output encoding and Content-Security-Policy. Both SQLi and XSS are INPUT-validation failures - a pairing exams love.

Man-in-the-Middle (MITM) positions the attacker between two parties, relaying and possibly altering traffic - enabled by unencrypted links (plain HTTP, open Wi-Fi). Defence: TLS everywhere. Related: session hijacking steals session cookies; replay attacks re-send captured legitimate traffic.

subsections.title: Defence mapping
subsections.content:
SQLi -> parameterised queries, least-privilege DB accounts.
XSS -> output encoding, CSP headers.
MITM -> TLS/HTTPS, VPN on public Wi-Fi.
Credential attacks -> MFA, lockouts, strong password policy.

quickRevision: SQLi = database commands via input; ' OR 1=1 -- is the classic payload.
XSS = malicious script on a trusted page; steals cookies.
MITM = secret relay between two parties; TLS kills it.
Both SQLi and XSS are input-validation failures.
tricks: 'Database' + 'input field' in the stem -> SQL injection.
patterns: ' OR 1=1 -- style payload shown in the stem -> SQLi.
'Injects malicious scripts into trusted websites' -> XSS.

pyqPatterns.question: Which attack injects SQL commands through input fields?
pyqPatterns.approach: SQL injection - the only database-execution attack in the options.

readingSections.companyNote: SQLi/XSS appear in the broader technical pool (and coding-round discussions); MITM pairs with VPN questions.

readingSections.title: Defence Mapping & Best Practices
readingSections.quickSummary: Every attack has a matching control: filters vs floods, training vs phishing, backups vs ransomware, TLS vs interception.
content: Security questions often run the arrow backwards: given an attack, name the defence. The mapping is logical: traffic floods meet firewalls/rate-limiting/anti-DDoS services; phishing meets user training and mail filtering; malware meets antivirus and patching; ransomware meets offline backups; interception meets encryption; credential guessing meets MFA and lockout policies.

Organisational practices wrap the technical controls: least privilege (minimum rights needed), defense in depth (many layers), regular patching (closing worm doors), security audits, and incident-response plans. The AXIS syllabus phrase 'organisational security' from the client-server topic lives here.
Zero Trust is the modern doctrine: never trust, always verify - every request authenticated and authorised regardless of network location.

subsections.title: The doctrine trio
subsections.content:
Least privilege - grant minimum rights needed.
Defense in depth - layered controls; no single wall.
Zero Trust - verify every request, every time.

quickRevision: Flood -> firewall/rate-limit. Phish -> training + mail filter. Malware -> AV + patches.
Ransomware -> offline backups. Interception -> TLS. Guessing -> MFA + lockouts.
Least privilege, defense in depth, zero trust - the doctrine trio.
tricks: Defence questions: pick the control that attacks the attack MECHANISM, not a neighbour.
'Never trust, always verify' is the Zero Trust slogan - quoted verbatim in options.
patterns: 'Best defence against ransomware' - regular offline backups.
'Best defence against phishing' - user awareness training.
'Verify every request regardless of origin' - Zero Trust.

pyqPatterns.question: Match the attack to its primary defence.

readingSections.companyNote: Defence-mapping items round out the security bucket - one usually appears alongside an identification question.

formulas.title: The Attack Identification Table

formula.text: Each one-line symptom maps to exactly one attack name - memorise the pairs verbatim.

explanation: Appears to be something else -> spoofing.
Unwanted mass emails -> email bombing.
Fraudulent messages stealing credentials -> phishing.
ICMP broadcast amplification with forged source -> smurfing.
Distributed traffic overwhelm -> DDoS.
Secret relay between two parties -> MITM.

example.prompt: User complains of thousands of junk emails.

formulas.memoryTip: Mail flood = bombing. Bandwidth flood = DoS. Fake face = spoofing.
formulas.commonMistake: Confusing phishing (targets people) with spoofing (forges identities).

formulas.title: The DoS Family Tree

formula.text: One attacker = DoS; thousands of coordinated attackers = DDoS; variants differ in the flood type.

explanation: SYN flood - half-open TCP connections exhaust the server table.
Smurf - ICMP to broadcast with spoofed source; replies swamp the victim.
Ping storm/ICMP flood - raw echo flooding.
DDoS - botnets coordinate thousands of sources; harder to block (no single origin).

example.prompt: Thousands of infected PCs flood one shop's checkout.

formulas.commonMistake: Calling a single-source flood a DDoS - the D needs distribution.

formulas.title: Malware Behaviour Matrix

formula.text: Four behaviours, four names - the discriminator is HOW it spreads and what it wants.

explanation: Virus: attaches to files; needs execution/sharing.
Worm: autonomous network replication; no host.
Trojan: disguised as useful software; user-installed.
Ransomware: encrypts data, demands payment.
Support cast: spyware (spies), keylogger (keystrokes), rootkit (hides), adware (ads).

example.prompt: Malware that spread with NO host file across the whole LAN overnight.

formulas.commonMistake: Saying viruses self-replicate over networks - that is the worm's signature.

formulas.title: SQLi & XSS: The Input-Validation Pair

formula.text: Both are input-validation failures; one hits the database, the other hits browsers.

explanation: SQLi: SQL fragments through inputs execute on the database; classic payload ' OR 1=1 --.
XSS: injected JavaScript runs in OTHER users' browsers; steals cookies/sessions.
Defence SQLi: parameterised queries, input validation.
Defence XSS: output encoding, Content-Security-Policy.

example.prompt: Login bypassed by typing ' OR 1=1 -- in the password box.

formulas.memoryTip: Database = SQLi. Browser = XSS. Both = validate input.
formulas.commonMistake: Calling cookie theft 'SQLi' - cookie/session theft is XSS's crime.

formulas.title: MITM & the TLS Counter

formula.text: Interception dies when both ends authenticate and encrypt - TLS certificates and VPN tunnels.

explanation: MITM relays/alters traffic between two parties secretly.
Enabled by plaintext links (HTTP, open Wi-Fi).
TLS certificates authenticate the server; encryption blinds the relay.
VPN extends that tunnel across untrusted networks.

example.prompt: Attacker reads logins on cafe Wi-Fi.

formulas.memoryTip: Open Wi-Fi + no TLS = eavesdropper's paradise.
formulas.commonMistake: Firewalls stopping MITM - filtering is not encryption; TLS is the counter.

formulas.title: Attack-to-Defence Mapping

formula.text: Match each attack mechanism to the control that breaks it.

explanation: DoS/DDoS -> firewalls, rate limiting, anti-DDoS services.
Phishing -> user training + mail filtering.
Malware -> antivirus + patching.
Ransomware -> offline/offsite backups.
Interception -> TLS/VPN. Credential guessing -> MFA + lockouts.
Doctrine: least privilege, defense in depth, zero trust.
formulas.memoryTip: Break the mechanism, not the neighbour.
formulas.commonMistake: Antivirus as the anti-phishing answer - phishing targets people, so training leads.

mcqs.q: An attack in which the user receives an unwanted amount of emails is:
mcqs.source: Asked in Accenture AXIS Technical Assessment
exp: Mail flood = email bombing.
Smurf/ping storm/DoS are bandwidth attacks.

mcqs.q: An attack in which a user creates a packet that appears to be something else is:
mcqs.source: Asked in Accenture AXIS Technical Assessment
exp: Forged identity at packet level = spoofing.
Trojan is disguised SOFTWARE, not a packet trick.

mcqs.q: Fraudulent messages that trick users into revealing credentials:
exp: Phishing deceives PEOPLE into handing over secrets.

mcqs.q: A DDoS attack differs from DoS because it:
exp: D = Distributed: botnets of thousands of machines swamp the victim.

mcqs.q: Which malware NEEDS a host file to spread?
exp: Viruses attach to host files and spread on execution.
Worms self-replicate over networks without hosts.

mcqs.q: Which malware self-replicates across networks WITHOUT a host file?
exp: Worms propagate autonomously - the network IS their vehicle.

mcqs.q: Malware disguised as legitimate software is a:
exp: The Trojan horse trick: useful-looking wrapper, malicious payload.

mcqs.q: Malware that encrypts data and demands payment:
exp: Ransom = pay-to-unlock extortion.

mcqs.q: Software that silently records keystrokes:
exp: Keyloggers capture credentials as they are typed.

mcqs.q: Typing ' OR 1=1 -- into a login field to bypass authentication is:
exp: The payload alters the backend SQL query - database attack = SQLi.

mcqs.q: Injecting malicious scripts into pages other users trust is:
exp: Cross-Site Scripting runs attacker JavaScript in VICTIMS' browsers - cookie theft follows.

mcqs.q: Secretly relaying and altering traffic between two parties is:
exp: MITM = the invisible postman who reads and edits letters.

mcqs.q: The primary defence against phishing is:
exp: Phishing exploits people - training plus filtering attacks that mechanism.

mcqs.q: The best defence against ransomware is:
exp: Restorable backups remove the extortion leverage.

mcqs.q: Which attack floods a service with traffic from thousands of infected machines?
exp: Botnets = distributed denial of service.

mcqs.q: Spyware's main purpose is to:
exp: Spyware watches and reports - espionage, not sabotage.

mcqs.q: ICMP echo requests sent to a broadcast address with a forged source is:
exp: Smurf = amplification: every broadcast host replies AT the spoofed victim.

mcqs.q: 'Never trust, always verify' is the slogan of:
exp: Zero Trust verifies every request regardless of network location.

mcqs.q: Granting users only the rights they need is:
exp: Least privilege shrinks the blast radius of any compromise.

mcqs.q: Which is a CREDENTIAL attack?
exp: Brute force grinds password combinations; MFA and lockouts counter it.

mcqs.q: Which malware turns infected PCs into DDoS soldiers?
exp: Bots await commands from a controller - coordinated floods on cue.

mcqs.q: Eavesdropping on network traffic is best countered by:
exp: Encrypted traffic is useless to a sniffer.

mcqs.q: Which attack targets a DATABASE through web input fields?
exp: SQLi = input fields as a database command line.

mcqs.q: Stolen session cookies are the typical prize of:
exp: Injected scripts read cookies -> session hijacking.

mcqs.q: A user receives an email 'from the bank' linking to a clone site that steals credentials. This is:
exp: Fake authority + fake page + credential harvest = textbook phishing.

mcqs.q: Which TWO techniques does a smurf attack combine?
exp: Forged source (spoofing) + broadcast echo amplification (ICMP) = the reply storm.

mcqs.q: Which malware pair is distinguished by host-file dependency?
exp: Virus needs the host file; the worm needs nothing but the network.

mcqs.q: An employee's browser runs attacker JavaScript that posts their session cookie to an external site. Attack?
exp: Script in a trusted page + cookie exfiltration = cross-site scripting.

mcqs.q: Which defence directly neutralises SQL injection?
exp: Parameterised queries separate code from data - injected fragments never execute.

mcqs.q: A botnet's controller is best described as:
opts: The command source coordinating infected machines
exp: Bot herder issues commands; the bots execute - DDoS on demand.

mcqs.q: Which attack re-sends captured legitimate traffic to gain access?
exp: Replays reuse valid transmissions; timestamps/nonces defeat them.

mcqs.q: Which malware buries itself in the OS to HIDE other malware?
exp: Root = deepest access; kit = toolkit - the stealth layer.

mcqs.q: An attacker emails a fake invoice with a malicious macro attachment. Two threats in one:
exp: The deceit is phishing; the attachment payload is trojan behaviour.

mcqs.q: Which control BEST limits the damage of a compromised account?
exp: Minimal rights = minimal blast radius.

mcqs.q: Which attack type is 'ping storm' closest to?
exp: Raw echo-request flooding - a DoS variant, distinct from smurf's broadcast trick.

mcqs.q: Output encoding and Content-Security-Policy defend against:
exp: Encoding neutralises injected scripts; CSP restricts what scripts may run.

mcqs.q: Which is a SOCIAL engineering attack (targets people, not machines)?
exp: Phishing hacks humans; the others hack systems.

mcqs.q: A forged email sender address (bank@secure-bank.example) that is not the real bank is:
exp: Forged FROM identity = spoofing at the mail layer (SPF/DKIM/DMARC counter it).

mcqs.q: Which layer of defence means 'many overlapping controls'?
exp: No single wall - layers upon layers.

mcqs.q: Which attack intercepts communication on open Wi-Fi to steal logins typed into HTTP sites?
exp: Plaintext over a shared medium = read-and-relay opportunities.

mcqs.q: Which malware demands cryptocurrency typically?
exp: Crypto payments are hard to trace - the ransom rail of choice.

mcqs.q: A 'drive-by download' infects a browser simply by VISITING a page. Primary defence?
exp: Unpatched browser vulnerabilities are the door; patching closes it.

mcqs.q: Which statement about DDoS mitigation is TRUE?
opts: Rate limiting and anti-DDoS services absorb/filter floods
exp: Filtering/scrubbing centres + rate limits absorb floods; bandwidth alone just raises the ceiling.

mcqs.q: Which attack uses a dictionary of common passwords?
exp: Automated guessing - lockouts and MFA are the counters.

mcqs.q: Which is an INSIDER threat example?
exp: Insider = trusted person misusing legitimate access.

mcqs.q: Multi-factor authentication primarily defeats:
exp: A stolen password alone is useless without the second factor.

mcqs.q: Which is TRUE about smurfing's amplification?
opts: Every broadcast host replies to the spoofed victim
exp: The forged source redirects the entire reply storm at the victim.

mcqs.q: Which practice closes the vulnerabilities worms exploit?
exp: Worms ride unpatched holes - patching shuts the doors.

mcqs.q: A published AXIS PYQ pairs 'unwanted amount of emails' with three traffic-attack distractors. The distractors work because all four are:
opts: Flooding attacks differing only in medium
exp: Smurfing, DoS and ping storm flood BANDWIDTH; email bombing floods a MAILBOX - the medium is the discriminator.

mcqs.q: An attacker cannot decrypt captured traffic but re-sends it later successfully. Which control would have prevented this?
exp: Replay attacks reuse valid captures; freshness tokens (nonce/timestamp) make replays stale.

mcqs.q: Which sequence correctly orders escalating malware defence?
opts: Antivirus -> patching -> offline backups -> network segmentation (random)
exp: Defense in depth: signature defence, vulnerability removal, containment, recovery - each layer covers the last's gaps.

mcqs.q: An attacker registers bank-secure-login.com and clones the bank's page. Which TWO defences catch this earliest?
exp: Phishing dies at human vigilance and mail authentication (SPF/DKIM/DMARC) - technical layers come later.

mcqs.q: Which attack does ENCRYPTION alone NOT stop?
exp: Ransomware executes WITH the user's rights on the endpoint - encryption protects data in transit/at rest, not local execution.

mcqs.q: A smurf attack's amplification factor equals:
opts: Number of hosts in the broadcast domain
exp: One request -> N hosts each reply to the victim: amplification = N.

mcqs.q: Which attack chain is internally consistent?
opts: Phishing email -> credential theft -> account misuse
exp: Only A follows cause-to-effect logically; the others mix incompatible mechanisms.

mcqs.q: Which control detects an active MITM on a LAN (ARP spoofing)?
exp: DAI validates ARP replies against trusted bindings - the direct counter to ARP spoofing.

mcqs.q: A worm outbreak is contained fastest by:
exp: Worms propagate over the network - cutting paths starves them; backups/training address other attacks.

mcqs.q: Which option pair lists an attack and its CORRECT direct counter?
opts: XSS -> output encoding; SQLi -> parameterised queries
XSS -> parameterised queries; SQLi -> output encoding
exp: Each input-validation failure has its specific fix - swapping them is the classic distractor.

mcqs.q: Why do DDoS attackers prefer botnets over single powerful servers?
opts: Distributed sources are harder to block and multiply total flood capacity
exp: Blocking one origin fails against thousands; capacity multiplies by node count.

mcqs.q: Map: 'invoice macro' -> ? ; 'fake bank page' -> ? ; 'broadcast ICMP storm' -> ?
exp: Attachment disguise = trojan delivery; cloned credential page = phishing; broadcast echo flood = smurfing.
Three table rows in one question - the AXIS style.
